newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Shotover sees profit, div in '98.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Shotover sees profit, div in '98.

text.p: Shotover Jet managing director Jim Boult on Monday slammed critics of his company's management following a NZ$3.9 million full-year loss, and said the tourism operator would return to profit and pay a dividend in the year to June 30, 1998.
"We'll be profitable this coming year. We've changed our balance date to June 30 and we'll be paying a dividend," Boult told Reuters in an interview.
Shotover recorded a trading surplus of NZ$974,000 for the year ended March 31 but writedowns of $4.9 million resulted in a $3.9 million loss for the period, and no dividend.

Boult said recent media reports had suggested Shotover's head office control was lax and its expansion haphazard, but he vigorously rejected this, saying only one mistake had been made. "The mistake we made was listening to some advice which said we were in too narrow an industry band, the jetboat business, and that we should be in tourism generally. That was a complete and utter balls-up, a complete mistake, and we're paying the price for it," he said.
Boult said the principal reason for the company's bottomline loss was its Rotorua tourist attractions Rainbow Springs and Rainbow Farm Show, purchased two years ago for $13 million.
"Rainbow has been a disaster for us, we accept that. We bought into it at a time when tourism patterns were changing dramatically and it's affected Rainbow's business incredibly."

The Christchurch Tramway attraction, in which Shotover has a 50.1 percent stake, had also not done as well as had been hoped. Shotover last week announced it would sell the Rainbow assets and return to its core focus of jetboating operations. Boult said the Tramway stake was also likely to be sold.

"The five year plan is to get rid of Rainbow for a start, and that will probably be followed by the Tramway since it's simply not our core business, which will take us back to the jetboating operations alone," he said.

"I would like to see us spend about two years consolidating the businesses that we have, a bit of fine tuning here and there, but minimising our capital expenditure to must-do items and giving our shareholders a decent dividend for a couple of years before we look at further overseas expansion."
Boult said the Rainbow millstone had forced Shotover to drop several exciting foreign projects, but it did plan to resume international expansion in time.

While he conceded Shotover could realistically expect to make a loss on the sale of the Rainbow assets, Boult said the company's operational profit was likely to exceed the surplus achieved last financial year.

"We're not very happy with the operational profit we made last year...there's certainly a lot of room to improve on that." Shotover's primary jetboating operation in Queenstown continued to make good money, the business in Fiji was doing
very well, and in Mexico revenue from the company's 50-percent held jetboating foray were starting to come on stream.
Furthermore, the Dart River Jet Safari business near Queenstown, acquired last year, was outperforming expectations.
"It's performed extremely well for us, well above expectation, it's continuing to do so, and that's the sort of place we should be expanding in," Boult said.

"We are the best jetboat company in the world fullstop. Last year this operation (Shotover in Queenstown) carried more passengers, made more money per passenger, had lower overheads per passenger and...it's probably the best marketed tourism
business in New Zealand," Boult said.
